title: Shopping South Water Street
premise: Complete a modest household list along the commercial riverfront without succumbing to every temptation on display.

opening.text:
JAUNT: SHOPPING SOUTH WATER STREET. This is the settlement's principal thoroughfare, and it is hardly picturesque: the river on one side, plank walks and mud on the other, and every establishment crammed with merchandise unloaded from the vessels. In 1833 the Democrat quoted tea at 87 cents to $1.25 a pound and calicos "from 15 to 38 cents" a yard.

You possess three dollars and a concise household list: something for a cough, a staple and tea. Three establishments on South Water supply them, and you will reconcile your purchases on Lake Street, where the town's commerce is migrating.

stops.text: Commence at Philo Carpenter's, the druggist at the Sign of the Golden Mortar. He disembarked in 1832 while cholera afflicted the fort, dispensed his drugs from a log house beside the river, and constructed this store the following summer. He also "prepared and circulated the first temperance pledge" in town, combining commerce with moral reform. His June notice enumerates aloes, ipecac, liquorice ball and tooth powder.

choices.label: Liquorice ball for a cough — 25¢
choices.consequence: A small paper of it is deposited in the basket alongside the household list.

stops.narrative: Purchase the remedy immediately, or trust that the household's cough eventually subsides independently.

stops.text: A short distance east, Peck's store occupies the corner of LaSalle and South Water. His 1833 advertisement enumerates dry goods, hardware, groceries and crockery, with fifty barrels of superfine flour in stock, and an 1834 notice supplements the inventory with flannels, ginghams and calicoes.

choices.label: Flour for the bin — $2
choices.consequence: The indispensable staple, consuming the majority of the purse.

choices.label: A length of calico — $1.25
choices.consequence: Cloth for mending, while the bread awaits a subsequent trip.

stops.narrative: Select the single staple the household requires most urgently, or conserve the purse.

stops.text: Further east at Clark Street stands Harmon, Loomis and Company, whose June 1835 notice offers Young Hyson and Souchong tea, loaf sugar, crockery and glassware. Andreas specifies the intersection of Clark and South Water, although not which corner. Their business is prospering: next year the firm will construct "the Harmon and Loomis block of four-story brick stores on South Water street".

choices.label: Young Hyson tea and loaf sugar — $1
choices.consequence: The concluding item on the list, accompanied by sugar.

choices.label: A smaller paper of Souchong — 40¢
choices.consequence: The purse is insufficient, so a more economical tea substitutes for the Hyson.

choices.label: A crockery bowl instead — 50¢
choices.consequence: Not on the list, but the household's bowl is cracked, so the tea is postponed.

stops.narrative: Compare the merchandise on the shelf with the funds remaining, and decide accordingly.

stops.text: Drive south along Clark to Lake Street, where in 1834, Moses and Kirkland write, business "began to extend to Lake street", and Thomas Church was among that year's arrivals. A modern note credits him with the first store building on this street, a two-story frame, although it specifies no merchandise, so nothing is purchased here. Reconcile your basket meticulously.
stops.narrative: Calculate what the basket contains and what the purse retains.

legs.note: A short drive east along the south side of South Water Street to Peck's corner at LaSalle.
legs.story: With the cough addressed, select the essential staple the household requires most urgently.

legs.note: The long leg: on east along South Water Street to Clark.
legs.story: Tea constitutes the final item on the list, and the purse is considerably depleted.

legs.note: South up Clark Street, away from the river, to Lake Street.
legs.story: With nothing further to purchase, locate a quiet spot away from the river and reconcile the expenditures.

endings.text: A staple, a remedy and tea: with the list completed and a few coins remaining, the household is provisioned for this week, and you comprehend South Water Street better than most newcomers.
A portion of the list must await another expedition, so you return home with whatever the purse permitted, and South Water Street, mud and all, will endure.

keepsake.title: The Household List
keepsake.text: A fictional household list and receipt from three South Water Street establishments, reconciled on Lake Street.

evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck advertised from the corner of LaSalle and South Water streets a stock of dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes and hats, with fifty barrels of superfine flour on hand; a later notice lists flannels, sattinetts, merino cloths, muslins, ginghams and calicoes.
evidence.locator: 3 Dec 1833, p. 3, col. 4 (Peck's card: stock and '50 bbls. Superfine FLOUR'); 10 Dec 1834, p. 4, col. 4 ('New Goods!!', the dry-goods summary ending in calicoes). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: Philo Carpenter advertised as a wholesale and retail druggist at the Sign of the Golden Mortar on South Water Street; in June 1835 his notice listed aloes, ipecac, liquorice ball, tooth powder and paste, perfumery, surgical instruments and trusses among his drugs and dye-stuffs.
evidence.locator: Chicago Democrat, 25 June 1834, p. 3, col. 2 (Carpenter's card, 'at the Sign of the Golden Mortar, South Water Street'); Chicago American, 27 June 1835, p. 3, col. 6 (the drug list, claim c013). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: Andreas has Carpenter buy a lot on South Water Street between LaSalle and Wells and erect a small store there in summer 1833; the lot within that block face is not recorded, and the marker stands at its middle.
evidence.reasoning: The block face is Andreas's; the mid-block point is the structure record's convention, not evidence. That this South Water store is the one the 1834-35 advertisements were written from is the record's continuity argument: the advertisements name the street and no lot.

evidence.text: Harmon, Loomis & Co. advertised wholesale and retail from their store in South Water Street: dry goods, hardware and cutlery, crockery and glass ware, Young Hyson, Hyson skin and Souchong teas, loaf and lump sugars and molasses.
evidence.locator: Chicago American, 20 June 1835, p. 1, col. 2 ('At Wholesale and Retail', claim c006); Chicago Democrat, 3 Sept 1834, p. 3, col. 5 ('New Goods—Again', loaf sugar and Hyson tea among the groceries). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: Andreas puts the Harmon and Loomis store at the corner of Clark and South Water and never says which corner; the marker's south-east corner is the structure record's choice.
evidence.reasoning: The north side of South Water was the river frontage and Andreas gives the south-west corner to the Chicago Democrat's office, so the record takes the south-east. The advertisements name South Water Street only.

evidence.text: An uncredited modern note says the first store building on Lake Street, a two-storey frame structure, was built by Thomas Church. It gives no year, no stock and no address, and this project grades the note as its weakest kind of source.
evidence.locator: Chicagology, early street maps gallery, the editorial addendum at the foot of the page: the Thomas Church sentence (accessed 2026-08-11).

evidence.text: Philo Carpenter landed at Chicago in July 1832, while cholera was at Fort Dearborn, and 'all ordinary intercourse had been suspended'; he leased 'a small log house standing near the river' and opened his store of drugs; the next summer he built a store on South Water Street between LaSalle and Wells and added salt, sugar and hardware.
evidence.locator: p. 572-573, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 100036-100121 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In 1832 Carpenter 'prepared and circulated the first temperance pledge among the convivial citizens of that early period'.
evidence.locator: p. 574, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 100255-100260 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The first numbers of the Democrat, in 1833, quote flour at $6 a barrel, butter at 17 cents a pound, tea at 87 cents to $1.25 a pound, loaf sugar 20 cents, coffee 17, 'whiskey 40 cents a gallon', and calicos 'from 15 to 38 cents' a yard.
evidence.locator: p. 93, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12620-12632 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Among the buildings of 1836 were 'the Harmon and Loomis block of four-story brick stores on South Water street'.
evidence.locator: p. 97, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13078-13082 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In 1834 'Business, which had heretofore been confined to South Water street on the South Side, began to extend to Lake street'; Thomas Church is among that year's arrivals who became leading citizens.
evidence.locator: p. 95, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12802-12821 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The source names Lake Street and nothing narrower; the store's place on the north side between LaSalle and Clark is a reconstruction.
Each store's stock is carried to 1 July 1835 from advertisements printed before it; none records a sale, a price or a customer on that day.
evidence.reasoning: Harmon, Loomis & Co. and Carpenter were both advertising in June 1835, days before the scene date. Peck's last card in the run is December 1834; he is attested keeping and living in this store across 1833-35, so his stock is carried forward from it.

evidence.text: The household list, the three-dollar purse, every price, the basket, the drive in a light wagon (the recommended mode), the two endings and The Household List keepsake are invented connective narrative, not historical events or prices. Each good is bought only from a store whose own advertisement lists it.
